name: MongoDB, Inc. (formerly 10gen)
origin_detail: Founded 2007 in New York City as 10gen by DoubleClick alumni Dwight Merriman, Kevin P. Ryan and Eliot Horowitz. It first aimed at a platform-as-a-service, scrapped it to focus on the database, released MongoDB as open source in February 2009 and renamed itself MongoDB Inc. on 2013-08-27.
openness_notes: Server was AGPL-3.0 (drivers Apache-2.0) from the 2009 release; the company later added proprietary enterprise features and the Atlas cloud service (open core). Versions released after 2018-10-16 are under the Server Side Public License v1, which is not OSI-approved; versions released before that remain AGPL. Drivers stay Apache-licensed, so the current level is 1 (source-available core).

license_history.note: Upstream swapped AGPL-3.0 for SSPL v1 on 2018-10-15/16; earlier versions remain AGPL.

relicensing_events.outcome_note: No direct community fork of the server gained traction. Debian (Dec 2018, package removed from unstable Feb 2020), Fedora and RHEL 8 (Jan 2019) dropped MongoDB as non-free. Compatibility alternatives grew instead: AWS DocumentDB (proprietary API-compatible service), FerretDB, and Microsoft's MIT-licensed Postgres-based DocumentDB, which joined the Linux Foundation on 2025-08-25 with AWS, Google, Cockroach Labs, Snowflake and Yugabyte backing.

exit_events.note: Priced 2017-10-18 at $24 (above a raised $20-22 range), 8.0M shares, raising $192M; opened at $33 and closed at $32.07 on 2017-10-19. Valuation estimates at pricing: ~$1.2B (Fortune), $1.17B basic, ~$1.39B fully diluted (Axios); below the ~$1.6B-1.7B last private valuation.

risk_events: 2018-10: SSPL relicense; Debian, Fedora and RHEL 8 dropped MongoDB; SSPL never became OSI-approved
2019 onward: hyperscaler API-compatible substitutes (AWS DocumentDB, later Microsoft's open DocumentDB at the Linux Foundation, Aug 2025)
2025-05: MongoDB began patent litigation against FerretDB, an open MongoDB-compatible project (reported by InfoQ, Nov 2026)
2025-11: Founder-era CEO Dev Ittycheria retired; Cloudflare's CJ Desai became CEO
2026-09-28: Desai stepped down effective immediately to join Meta; Ittycheria returned as interim CEO while a search runs
robustness: Single-vendor control, no foundation. Revenue is now mostly Atlas/subscription ($2.39B of $2.46B in FY2026) and the company is cash-generative ($505M operating cash flow FY2026), but leadership has been unstable in 2025-2026. The wire protocol is now reimplemented by open, foundation-hosted alternatives (DocumentDB at the Linux Foundation), which reduces customer lock-in and MongoDB's moat.
physical_science_relevance: Widely used as a schemaless store for lab and sensor data; this lab's own digital-wetlab uses MongoDB Atlas.
openness_effect_assessment: AGPL openness drove early developer adoption that the company converted into one of the largest open-source-origin IPOs of 2017. Closing to SSPL in 2018 did not stall growth: revenue rose to $2.46B in FY2026 and the market cap sits around $23B, because Atlas (its own hosting) became the main revenue line. The costs were reputational and ecosystem-level: distributions dropped it, and hyperscalers responded with compatible substitutes that in 2025 moved into a neutral Linux Foundation project.
key_takeaway: MongoDB is the clearest case of an open-source-origin company that closed its license and still kept growing: SSPL protected its managed-service business from cloud resale, and the market rewarded it with roughly a 20x rise from its IPO valuation. But closing the license did not remove competition, it moved it to the API layer, where the hyperscalers now back an MIT-licensed, foundation-governed alternative. For an openness study, MongoDB shows that a strong first-party cloud product, not the license, is what captures value, while openness mainly bought the early adoption.
